Unit 02 — Cash vs. Profit: why a "profitable" company can still run out of money

4 min read954 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06learn/unit-02-cash-vs-profit.md

  2. ① Material — what we're learning, and where it lives

For a beginner. Builds on Unit 01. Same company (Royal Caribbean), same event (COVID), one new idea: profit and cash are not the same thing — and confusing them is how people get fooled.

Plain words first (read once)

  • Revenue / profit (net income) — revenue = money customers paid in; profit (a.k.a. net income) = what's left after all costs. (From Unit 01.)
  • Operating cash flow (OCF) — the actual cash the company's normal business brought in this year.
  • Non-cash charge — a cost on paper that no cash actually paid this year (depreciation is the big one).
  • Depreciation — spreading the cost of a big long-lived thing (a ship, a van) across the years it's used, as a yearly expense — even though the cash went out when it was bought.
  • "Booked" a sale — recorded a sale in the accounts, which can happen before the customer pays.
  • 10-K / SEC / EDGAR — a company's annual report, filed with the SEC (the U.S. regulator) and free on its EDGAR website. · $X B = X billion dollars.

① Material — what we're learning, and where it lives

Unit 01 used the income statement (revenue → profit). Now meet the second scoreboard: the cash flow statement, which answers a different question — did real money actually come in? The top of it we care about is operating cash flow (OCF): the cash the core business threw off this year. It sits in every 10-K, right after the income statement, free on EDGAR.

② Understanding — the idea in plain language

Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. Profit follows accounting rules that include things where no money moved this year. The big one is depreciation:

Your lemonade stand buys a $12,000 delivery van that lasts about 6 years. Accounting won't subtract all $12,000 from this year's profit — it spreads the cost as a ~$2,000-a-year "expense" across those 6 years (6 × $2,000 = $12,000). You paid the full $12,000 cash up front, but in the later years your profit keeps showing a ~$2,000 cost while no cash leaves at all. In those years your cash is higher than your profit by that $2,000 — the expense is real on paper, but the money already left long ago.

It runs the other way too: if a customer promises to pay (sale booked, cash not yet in your hand), profit goes up but no cash arrived. So:

  • Profit can be higher than cash (e.g., booking sales customers haven't paid yet).
  • Cash can be higher than profit (e.g., depreciation — a paper cost, no cash out).

Why it matters, bluntly: companies don't die from low profit; they die from running out of cash. You must watch both lines.

③ Example — Royal Caribbean's real numbers (the two come apart)

From RCL's actual filings (USD):

Year Profit (net income) Operating cash flow What it shows
2019 +$1.9 B +$3.7 B Cash was nearly double profit — because ships depreciate (a paper cost, no cash out).
2020 −$5.8 B −$3.7 B COVID: the loss was real in cash too — the business bled billions.
2022 −$2.2 B +$0.5 B The punchline: a net loss, but cash flow turned positive. Profit and cash had opposite signs.

Read it: - 2019 is pillar ②'s "cash > profit" lesson, live: $3.7B of cash vs. $1.9B of profit — the ~$1.8B gap is largely depreciation on those giant ships (a real expense, no cash leaving), plus other non-cash and timing items. - 2020 shows the other truth: when the event hit, the loss was cash-real — they actually drained billions, which is why they had to borrow to survive (that's Unit 03). - 2022 is the one to remember: the income statement said "still losing money" (−$2.2B), but the cash flow said "the boats are sailing and cash is coming in again" (+$0.5B). If you only watched profit, you'd have missed that the business had already turned the corner on cash.

④ Application — your turn

A. Compute. In 2019, profit was $1.9B and operating cash flow was $3.7B. How big was the gap, and what mostly explains it? (≈ $1.8B; largely depreciation — a non-cash expense — plus timing items.)

B. Explain. In 2022 the company reported a loss but positive operating cash flow. In one sentence, why is that possible? (Profit includes non-cash charges like depreciation; the actual cash the sailings generated was positive even though the accounting bottom line was still negative.)

C. Reason it out (no computer needed). A software company reports a $200M profit and $260M of operating cash flow. Which is bigger, and name the most likely reason. (Cash is bigger — a non-cash charge like depreciation reduced profit but didn't take cash out this year.)

D. Optional — pull it yourself (only if you have this project set up). With the repo running you can compare any company's profit vs. cash: python3 _ingest/edgar.py facts COST. No setup? Skip it — A–C already taught the skill.

Check yourself

  1. A company reports a $50M profit but negative operating cash flow. Name one way that happens. (e.g., it booked sales customers haven't paid for yet — profit up, cash not in.)
  2. Which line tells you whether a company can survive next month — profit or cash? (Cash.)
